The Postmaster General recommends this order in recognition of Mr. Sauls' bravery in protecting Government property on the night of January 7, 1910. While acting as watchman in the post office at Tallahassee, Fla., Mr. Sauls was attacked by two masked burglars, both of whom, after a desperate fight, were killed. One of these burglars was a notorious yeggman who had robbed many post offices and had various indictments pending against him. On account of the appropriation act providing 'that rewards may be paid only for the arrest and conviction of post office robbers, Mr. Sauls can not be paid a reward by the Government. May 16, 1914. The superintendent of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings is hereby authorized to promote Mr. Willara H. Wheeler to the position of watchman on the watch force of the State, War, and Navy Department Buildings, independently of Wheeler's being regularly certified for such promotion under the civil-service rules. Wheeler, who is now a laborer under the same office, has a commendable military record to his credit, and recently in the line and the proper performance of his present duties suffered an injury to his left hand which has appreciably and permanently impaired his usefulness in doing the heavier work required of the laborer force.

October 29, 1914. Edward A. Gisburne may be appointed to a classified position without reference to his physical condition after recommendation by some appointing officer and such noncompetitive examination as the Civil Service Commission may require. Mr. Gisburne was a messenger boy in the classified service of the Navy Department from September 14, 1908, to February 7,1910, when he resigned to enlist in the Navy. He was honorably discharged from the Navy on August 29, 1914, by reason of disability resulting from wounds incurred in the line of duty, and was awarded a medal of honor for attempting to save a comrade while wounded himself. Under the law heis entitled to preference in original appointment if found, upon examination, to possess the required business capacity. This action is taken upon the request of the postmaster at Boston, Mass., and the Executive order is recommended by the Civil Service Commission.

February 10, 1916. Mr. Joseph W. Harris may be reinstated as fourth assistant examiner in the Patent Office, the year limit of eligibility for reinstatement being waivea in his case. Mr. Harris is said by the Secretary of the Interior to have proved particularly efficient in cases involving metallurgy and electro chemistry during his service of nearly six years in the Patent Office, and to have been contin- uously engaged in prosecuting applications for patents from his resignation on April 3, 1912, to the present time, thus having had an experience of nearly 10 years in patent work. In view of the technical character of the position and the experience of Mr. Harris, and his evident qualifications for the position, the commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending an Executive order to permit his reinstatement.

November 1, 1913. Mrs. Florence Kugler, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed as a clerk, class 1, in the Bureau of Pensions, Department of the Interior, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Kugler is the widow of Wellington Kugler, who served for over 20 years as a clerk in the Quartermaster’s Department, United States Army, and died February 11, 1911, at San Antonio, Tex., while still serving in that capacity. Mr. Kugler was a clerk in the office of the Adjutant General, and was injured at the time of the collapse of the Ford Theater building, which was occupied by the Record and Pension Office under the Adfan General. A board of surgeons afterwards reported that Mr. Kugler was three-fourths permanently injured. He never recovered from the effects of the disaster, and in the opinion of the doctors and his family the injuries thus received hastened his death. rs. Kugler was appointed to a temporary position in the Bureau of Pensions September 6, 1912, for a period of 60 days. On November 6, 1912, the appointment was extended until further notice. On May 20, 1913, former Commissioner Daven- port reported that all appointments on the temporary roll would expire the 30th day of June and that Mrs. Kugler had an excellent record and had performed her duties in an exceptionally efficient manner. On June 20, 1913, Commissioner Saltzgaber reported that, after an interview with Mrs. Kugler and an examination of her record, which he found most excellent, he cordially indorsed her application for an Executive order. For the above reasons this order is issued authorizing the appointment of Mrs. Kugler to a position in the classified service. Her husband, the late Mr. Kugler, entered the service of the Government on March 1, 1889.

February 14, 1917. : Mrs. Nora A. Fennell may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. Mrs. Fennell served as a printer’s assistant and operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing continuously from March 12, 1900, to April 16, 1903, when she resigned“to be married. It appears from the statement of the Secretary of the Treasury that Mrs. Fennell is a widow with three children dependent upon her for support, and that she is still a young woman in excellent health and capable of ren- dering in the future, as she rendered in the past, efficient service. The register of eligibles for original appointment to the position of printer’s assistant is practically exhausted, for which reason and in view of the other facts above an the com- mission, concurs with the Secretary of the Treasury in a recommendation for an Execu- ' tive order. :

Executive order Mr. John M. Savage, of New Jersey, formerly vice and deputy consul at Belfast, Ireland, from October i, 1885, to 1889, and vice consul and consul at Dundee, Scotland, from October 6, 1893 until the fall of 1 897, when he was summarily removed from his position, may be appointed to a post in the consular service without regard to the Executive Order of June 27, 1906. It appears from the records of the State Department that an inspec- tion of Mr. Savage's office in 1896, resulted in a report to the Department that the office wvas in excellent order. Mr. Savage is under fifty years of age, the limit fixed in the Executive Order of June 27, 1906, for applicants who desire to take the examination. WOODROW WILSON THE WHITE HOUSE, 21 April, 1914. [No. 1918.]

October 22, 1913. Mr. Edward W. Cronin may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. r. Cronin was appointed to the Railway Mail Service on August 14, 1901, and retained in the service until March 29, 1902, when he was dropped from the service. His reinstatement is recommended by the Postmaster General, who states that his separation from the service does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. The (Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case. :

November 10, 1914. Mr. W. T. Bateman may be appointed a watchman in a navy yard without compli- ance with the civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who says the case is a deserving one and that the general character of Mr. Bateman 1s such that he feels justified in recommending an exemption from the civil-service rules which will permit his employment in a navy yard so that he may be able to support his family. It appears that Mr. Bateman, seaman, formerly attached to the U. S. S. Foote, is at present a patient in the Naval Hospital, Washington, D. C. While visiting his family a l-pounder shell which he was showing his child exploded and blew off his left hand. The Surgeon General of the Navy concurs in the recommendation of the Sec- retary of the Navy and says Mr. Bateman is a very deserving man. While Mr. Bate- man will be discharged from the Navy for disability he can receive no pension, as his disability was not incurred in the line of duty. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of the order. Mr. Bateman has been employed temporarily at the navy yard since July 1, 1906.

Grant may be reinstated to a position in the classified service in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of time she has been sep- arated from the service. Mrs. Grant, as Mrs. Lillie B. Silcott, was appointed to the position of printer's assistant in the Bureau of Printing and Engraving on August 2, 1895, and was pro- moted to operative and through the several grades of that position. On July 1, 1902, she was transferred to the Post Office Department as clerk at |900, and was promoted to $1,000 July 1, 1905. She resigned May 9, 1912. Moran may be appointed as a clerk-typewriter in the office of the Chief of Ordnance, War Department, at $900 per annum, without reference to the re- quirement of examination under the civil-service rules. The appointment of Miss Moran is recommended by the Chief of the Bureau of Ordnance and the Acting Secretary of War, for the reason that she has had consider- able experience in Government work while temporarily employed in the Bureaus of Animal Industry and Forestry, Department of Agriculture, and the Patent Office,

October 17, 1916. : Mrs. George S. Ferrow may be appointed to an existing vacancy in the position of clerk at $900 per annum in the Bureau of Navigation, Department of Commerce, with- out reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Commissioner of Navigation, who state that Mrs. Ferrow is the widow of Mr. George S. Ferrow who died on October 2, 1916, as a result of an accident, and who was in charge of an important section of the Bureau of Navigation; that for many years he served in various capacities and was at all times a faithful, efficient, and industrious clerk; that as a result of his death his widow and two small children have been left without means of support; that Mrs. Ferrow is fully competent to perform the duties of the position to which it is proposed to appoint her; and that for these reasons it is believed that an exception to the rules in her case is warranted in the interest of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

December 7, 1914. Miss Louisa W. Happersett may be appointed to a position in the classified civil service without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that the Quartermaster General, the Surgeon General, and the Judge Advocate General of the Army unite in requesting the issuance of an Executive order. Miss Happersett is the daughter of the late John C. G. Happersett, major and surgeon, United States Army, who rendered highly efficient military service during a period of 32 years, including the 4 years of the Civil War. The Surgeon General and the Judge Advocate General call special attention to the services rendered by Maj. Happersett and his family during the yellow-fever epidemic at Fort Brown, Tex., in 1882. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending the order. Miss Happersett was appointed a copyist in the War Department on June 15, 1893, and served until 1905.

July 30, 1913. Mr. Frank E. Anderson may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Bureau of Pensions, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his sepa- ration from the service. Mr. Anderson entered the service through open competitive examination in 1884 and was dismissed on April 30, 1897. The official who recommended his dismissal subsequently recommended his reinstatement by Executive order, but it was not accomplished. The Civil Service Commission reviewed his case and considered it to be most deserving. President Roosevelt expressed the desire that the reinstatement be made. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the issuance of this order on account of Mr. Anderson’s demonstrated efficiency and extended experience in the work of the Pension Bureau, and in view of the foregoing facts the Civil Service Commission con- curs, as the order merely waives the year limit under the reinstatement rule. 45976°—14——9

June 28, 1917. Mr. H. H. Chapman may be reinstated as assistant district forester under the Department of Agriculture without regard to the year limitation upon eligibility for reinstatement. Mr. Chapman worked as a student assistant in the Forest Service as early as 1899. In July, 1904, he was appointed forest assistant through appropriate examination, and continued in this position until 1906, when he was appointed instructor in the Yale Forest School, and the following year became an assistant professor. At various intervals or during summer vacations between 1906 and 1910 he was employed by the department as a collaborator. His resignation from the Forest Service was effected in February, 1914. Since his separation from the service, his work has been along lines tending to enhance his value to the Government. He is considered one of the best foresters in the country, and in the opinion of the department the best interests of the service will be met by his reemployment. The commission concurs in recommending the order.

August 16, 1915. Miss Edna M. Ricketts, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the classified service of the Government without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Ricketts is the daughter of the late Thomas T. Ricketts, a veteran of Company C, Thirty-ninth Ohio Volunteer Infantry, who was an employee in the Government Printing Office from July, 1900, until the time of his death in April, 1913. She is an experienced stenographer and typewriter, and is the sole support of her widowed mother (now 74 years of age). : The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case.

May 7, 1917. Mrs. Annie Eopolucci may be appointed to a position as seamstress at the Wash- ington Navy Yard, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Eopolucci is the mother of John I. Eopolucci, formerly an enlisted man in the Navy, who was detailed as a gunner on the Aztec, and was the first person in the naval service of the United States to lose his life as the result of the sinking of an armed merchantman.

November 16, 1915. Mr. Charles Hardin may be reinstated as a clerk at not to exceed $1,200 per annum in the Post Office Department without regard to the length of his sepa- ration from the service. Mr. Hardin was appointed August 15, 1887, through appropriate examination as a clerk at $900 in the Post Office Department at Washington, and was removed from the position of clerk, class 8 ($1,600), on January 26, 1901, for irregularities in connection with the dead-letter sale. The records of the department show that Mr. Hardin's removal was based on the report and recommendation of a post-office inspector who investigated the charges. The Postmaster General reports that this report, which it is under- stood was favorable to Mr. Hardin, was apparently extracted from the files by the previous administration. He further states that as it is believed that the removal of Mr. Hardin, and the manner by which he was removed, was unjust to him, the department feels that it would be in the interest of justice to rein- state him. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case.
